title: I shipped a 3D iOS game in 2 weeks with Claude Code: 10 chapters, ~70k lines of C#, zero AI-generated art
author: dkingalon
selftext:
**Pillar of Fire: Bible Legends**: ten Bible stories as short 3D chapters, each with its own mechanic: a rhythm-timed sling against Goliath, a march to the drum round Jericho, fire on Elijah's altar, walking through the Red Sea. From first commit to App Store review took about 2 weeks.

**How the work was split**

* I did the design, the content calls and all the judging of feel and looks on the device, chapter by chapter, from playtest notes.
* Claude Code wrote the code: gameplay, UI, the build scripts, and the App Store Connect uploads.

**What made it work with an agent**

* **Everything is code, nothing is hand-placed.** All the scenes come from C# builder scripts. To fix a scene, the agent edits its builder and regenerates. The diffs stay reviewable and nothing drifts.
* **Art is code too, on top of CC0 kits.** The clothes are generated meshes on a CC0 character kit, and the trees, rocks and walls come from shared mesh builders. The lion and bear are a Blender Python script run headless. No image models anywhere: the agent can't see style the way I can, but it can build shapes it can measure, and I judge the renders.
* **An automated playtester as its eyes.** Play-mode tests drive the game with a scripted finger at human reaction times, log events, and save contact sheets of frames. Another script checks every recording for bodies that float, sink, slide or pass through things. The agent reads those before telling me something works. Feel stays my call on the phone.
* **One progress file as memory.** The to-dos, open decisions and a dated log are read at the start of every session and updated at the end, so context survives between sessions.

**What it was bad at:** taste. Its first menus looked like every other generic "premium" UI (rounded dark cards, gold pill buttons). It got good once I wrote down the visual rules and rejected things specifically.

**The trailer** was filmed by the playtests too: they record each chapter's set piece with game time stepped at exactly 1/30 s per frame. A script then adds the verses and the end card in ffmpeg.

Happy to answer anything about the workflow or get feedback from you!
